title: The CFO who topped the chart, and why that was wrong

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In one notebook, the best-paid job in Canada was a bilingual receptionist in Simcoe County. Senior range: sixty-three thousand to seven hundred thirteen thousand dollars.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a very good receptionist job. Or a typo.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A typo, probably seventy-one point three in the original. And that's one of the bugs Antoine found when he re-read a 2023 Canadian salary guide, using text already extracted in a GitHub project called Salary.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nineteen thousand three hundred eighty-seven rows with salary ranges, from a recruitment firm's guide, across fifty-six named regions. The extraction tagged every cell by heading level, so he could rebuild the tables.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Finance and HR tables don't have entry, mid and senior columns. Some have one, three, five and ten years of experience, and others have company revenue. The scraper assumed three experience levels everywhere, so a chief financial officer at a thousand-million-dollar company showed up as a senior salary, topping the maximum chart. Also, industrial support jobs like pickers and drivers were quoted per hour, but mixed with annual salaries, which dragged every average down.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So after cleaning, what does the guide say?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Technology pays the most, with a median mid-level figure of ninety-seven thousand two hundred, about fifteen thousand above engineering. Senior pay for the median job is about one point three times entry pay. And for the same job, Montréal, Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary land within about ten percent of each other for developers and architects.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He warns against them. Each region lists its own jobs, so a province median compares baskets, not salaries. Alberta came first and Prince Edward Island last, but that mostly reflects which jobs are listed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Any caveat on the numbers themselves?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. They're a recruitment firm's quoted ranges, not observed pay. They say what the firm quotes, not what people earn.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So read the tables correctly before you trust the chart.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the lesson. The full write-up has the charts and the list of fixes for the repository.
